grammar.note_en:
The same place prepositions now distinguish a destination from a location. Compare Mira legt das Heft auf die Bank (“Mira lays the notebook onto the bench”) with Das Heft liegt auf der Bank (“The notebook lies on the bench”). The first phrase names the destination the notebook reaches; the second names its resulting position. Direction takes accusative: den for masculine, die for feminine, das for neuter. Location keeps the dative from chapter6: dem, der, dem. The feminine forms differ in their articles too: auf die Bank versus auf der Bank.

Movement alone does not decide the case. Ben fährt auf der Straße (“Ben rides on the street”) locates the riding on the street, so it takes dative. Er fährt in den Hof (“He rides into the courtyard”) names a destination and takes accusative. Later Er fährt auf die Straße (“He rides out onto the street”) names a new destination. A verb such as gehen or fahren can therefore appear with either case, depending on what the place phrase means. The same distinction works with in, an, auf, unter, neben, hinter, vor and zwischen; these are the two-way prepositions encountered here.

Stellt describes placing something upright: Mira stellt den Koffer neben die Tür (“Mira places the case beside the door”). Steht describes its position: Der Koffer steht neben der Tür (“The case stands beside the door”). Legt describes laying something flat; liegt describes lying there. Setzt describes seating someone: Nora setzt das Kind auf den Stuhl (“Nora seats the child on the chair”); sitzt describes the child’s resulting position. Each placement has a direct object (den Koffer, das Heft, das Kind) and a separate destination phrase. The accusative object does not control the article after the preposition.

Each noun in a zwischen phrase receives its own article: Ben stellt den Stuhl zwischen den Tisch und das Fenster (“Ben puts the chair between the table and the window”), then Der Stuhl steht zwischen dem Tisch und dem Fenster (“The chair stands between the table and the window”). The destination changes both articles to accusative; the resulting location uses dative for both. Ins is the normal contraction of in das, as in Sie geht ins Haus (“She goes into the house”). Compare im Haus = in dem Haus (“in the house”). An das Fenster remains two words here; its location is am Fenster = an dem Fenster.

Hinein points into an interior, hinaus out of it, and zurück back to a previous position. These short directions need no noun or article: Mira geht hinein (“Mira goes in”). The hin- forms are used here to direct attention away from the speaker’s current reference position; they do not license other particle verbs or commands. Links, rechts and geradeaus mean “left,” “right” and “straight ahead”; the direction picture looks the same way Mira does, into the shop.

Bringt means “brings”: someone carries an object to a destination. Holt means “fetches”: the person goes to get it and returns with it. The story enacts the whole round trip before you practise holt. Fährt marks travel by vehicle; Ben is riding a bicycle. Läuft here describes the child running. The finite forms in the vocabulary cards are the ones actually read; their dictionary forms are stellen, legen, setzen, bringen, holen, fahren and laufen. Regular personal endings continue in ich stelle, ich setze, ich bringe, du bringst and ich hole. In questions, du stellst follows the same regular pattern as ich stelle and sie stellt; it has no stem change.

Jetzt means “now.” In the repeated pattern Jetzt ist der Weg frei (“Now the way is clear”), jetzt fills the first position and ist follows it, before the subject. This chapter only practises that familiar jetzt + ist pattern; fuller fronting and its word order belong to the next chapter. Frei can describe an unobstructed route or an available place. Nora sees space for boxes where Mira and Lina see a shared reading table. No boxes have been carried into the shop by the end; Nora has announced what she intends to do.
